setup.title: Setup and scan subnets
setup.summary: On the first start a wizard walks you through what is needed: networks, first scan, admin password.
setup.steps:
Open http://<host>:8000 and finish the setup wizard right after the first start.
The wizard detects the host's networks and saves them as scan subnets. Networks behind the router, such as an IoT VLAN, can be added in the same step.
It sets the admin password and runs the first scan.
Later you manage the list under Settings → Scan subnets: add, pause, remove.
setup.hint: Until the wizard is finished, whoever opens the page first chooses the admin password. So finish it right after the start.

https.title: HTTPS with a reverse proxy
https.summary: Without HTTPS the one-line installer installs no agent, and terminal keystrokes cross the network unencrypted.
https.steps:
Put a reverse proxy in front of GravityLAN, e.g. Caddy, Nginx Proxy Manager or Traefik, and forward an address like gravitylan.example.com to http://<host>:8000.
The proxy has to pass WebSockets through: the SSH terminal, the live log and the scan progress use them. Caddy and Traefik do it by themselves; in Nginx Proxy Manager turn on "Websockets Support".
Use a certificate your hosts trust, most easily Let's Encrypt through your domain's DNS challenge, which needs no port open to the internet. A self-signed certificate only works if every agent host knows its CA, because curl and the agent check certificates.
Under Settings → System, enter the "Agent server URL" with https://. Without it GravityLAN only knows its own http address, and new agents would report unencrypted.
Set GRAVITYLAN_SECURE_COOKIES=true on the container so the login cookie is only sent over HTTPS.
https.hint: Over http:// the one-line installer stops with a message. ALLOW_INSECURE=1 or GRAVITYLAN_ALLOW_INSECURE_INSTALL=true forces it anyway, but then the agent script and its token cross the network unencrypted. Installing over SSH works without HTTPS too.

dashboard.title: Overview and groups
dashboard.summary: All devices in your own sections, as tiles or a list, with live values from the agent.
dashboard.steps:
New devices show up in the IP overview first; "On dashboard" brings them into the overview.
Create, rename and sort groups under Settings → Groups. In the device editor you put a device into a group.
In edit mode you move and resize tiles; React and GravityUI share the positions.
Search (Ctrl+K) finds devices by name, IP, MAC or service.
dashboard.hint: Service badges open a device's web UI in one click; for SMB the path is copied.

ip.title: IP overview, VLANs and gateways
ip.summary: Every subnet as a map of its addresses, and how GravityLAN reaches it.
ip.steps:
Every scan subnet has its own tab with all addresses: used, free, online, offline, reserved.
Clicking an address opens details and actions: reserve, monitor, rename, bring to the dashboard, port scan.
The badge on a subnet shows the way: L2 Direct (own interface), L3 Routed (through the router) or L2 Probe (through an agent inside it).
In the subnet settings you store gateway and VLAN tag. A router that is the gateway of several VLANs stays one device with one interface per network.
ip.hint: In routed networks a scan cannot see MAC addresses. For real MACs and vendors use an agent as a Layer-2 probe or the multi-VLAN Docker Compose variant.

router.title: Import networks from the router
router.summary: Take scan subnets and VLANs straight from your router.
router.steps:
Settings → Scan subnets → Import from router.
Pick the way: SNMP (v1, v2c or v3, read-only) fits OPNsense, pfSense, OpenWrt, MikroTik and most business routers; there is also the official UniFi Network API.
The preview lists every network with gateway, name and VLAN. Only what you select is added.
For subnets you already have, only an empty gateway or VLAN is filled in.
router.hint: The import never overwrites names and values you set yourself.

topology.title: Topology and racks
topology.summary: How everything connects: as an orbit map or in the rack.
topology.steps:
The topology shows your network as a solar system: the router is the star, switches and hosts orbit as planets, endpoints as moons.
"Edit orbit" lets you drag devices, connect them with light beams and set link type and colour.
In the inspector you choose a device's role (star, planet, dwarf planet, moon) and the hub it orbits.
The "Rack view" shows your racks. Drag a device from "Without a rack" onto a free unit, or click it and then the free place; a double click opens the device editor.
topology.hint: A fixed colour per connection type (10GbE, 1GbE, WLAN …) is set in Settings.

agent.title: Install and update the agent
agent.summary: One Python script per Linux host reports CPU, RAM, disks, network and temperature.
agent.steps:
Open the device in the device editor, tab "Agent".
Over SSH: pick a saved key connection or type in user and password. Typed-in credentials are used for that request only.
Or copy the one-line installer and run it on the host. It carries a one-time code valid for 30 minutes.
Without HTTPS the one-liner stops (see "HTTPS with a reverse proxy"); installing over SSH works anyway.
Updates: the Agent Update Center updates all outdated agents together, and an open SSH terminal offers an "Agent update" button.
agent.hint: The agent version only changes when the agent script changes. Not every server update needs an agent update.

updates.title: Package updates
updates.summary: The agent counts pending updates (apt, dnf, yum); they are installed over SSH with live output.
updates.steps:
Agents page → open a host's row → Updates.
Sign in with a password, a key or a stored key.
Check the package list, then install security updates only or all of them; the output runs live.
As a non-root user with a key, enter the sudo password in its own field if sudo asks for one.
updates.hint: Without a sudo password it only works when sudo is passwordless for that user (NOPASSWD). Otherwise the update stops right away with a clear message.

ssh.title: SSH terminal and stored keys
ssh.summary: Shells on your devices in the browser, also on phones.
ssh.steps:
On the SSH page pick a saved connection, reopen a recent one or enter a host directly.
On the first connect you check the host key. If it changes later, GravityLAN warns and blocks the connection.
In the key store you import or generate keys (OpenSSH, PEM, PuTTY .ppk); they are stored encrypted on the server.
Tabs stay open while you use other pages. Right-click offers copy, paste and "copy last command".
ssh.hint: Back up data/ssh_vault.key (or GRAVITYLAN_VAULT_KEY) on its own: without it, stored keys can no longer be decrypted.

health.title: Health Radar
health.summary: Availability, latency and incidents of all devices at a glance.
health.steps:
Pick the period: 24 hours, 7 or 30 days.
The table shows status, score, uptime bars, latency with jitter and services per device; a click opens the details.
The details show the latency history, services with SSL expiry, agent values and incidents.
Turn off 24/7 monitoring for clients like a TV or laptop. Asleep, they then count as standby instead of an outage.
health.hint: Incidents of the last 7 days are listed below as a timeline; clicking a card opens the device.

telemetry.title: Measurement data and retention
telemetry.summary: Measurements live in their own telemetry.db and are condensed over time.
telemetry.steps:
Raw values (health probes and agent reports) are kept 48 hours by default.
Then they are folded into hourly values (30 days) and daily values (365 days).
Settings → Measurement data shows the database sizes and the retention per tier.
You can delete values older than N days, those of one device or everything; the space goes back to the file system.
telemetry.hint: Measurement data is not part of backups and exports, which keeps the inventory small.

api.title: API tokens and webhooks
api.summary: Query data through the REST API, connect an AI assistant and get notified about events.
api.steps:
Settings → API tokens: create a token. Tokens are read-only; finer rights are granted through the API.
The API documentation with Swagger UI is at /docs.
For an AI assistant or agent (for example Hermes or Clawdbot), a read-only token is enough: it reads devices, topology, health and agent metrics, but never gets SSH, agent configuration or admin endpoints.
Webhooks for device.offline and scan.complete are created through the API (/api/webhooks).
For Python there is the gravitylan_api client (pip install ./gravitylan_api from the repository).
api.hint: Webhooks cannot target GravityLAN itself, link-local addresses or cloud metadata; LAN addresses work.

backup.title: Backup and restore
backup.summary: Save devices, groups and settings as JSON and restore them.
backup.steps:
Settings → Backup & restore → Export downloads a JSON file.
Take a backup before every update.
Import restores devices, groups and settings.
The admin password, the master token and the setup state are never touched by an import.
backup.hint: SSH keys, stored passwords and agent tokens are not in the backup. Back up data/ssh_vault.key on its own.

unraid.title: Unraid, PUID and PGID
unraid.summary: The container prepares its data directory itself.
unraid.steps:
The Unraid template sets PUID=99 and PGID=100 (nobody:users, the appdata default).
On start the container hands /app/data to that user and starts the server as it.
A fresh appdata folder owned by root works without chown.
If you set a user with --user, give the folder to that user or remove --user; the container log names the UID and GID.
unraid.hint: Images up to 0.5.2 run as UID 1000. There, a one-time chown -R 1000:1000 /mnt/user/appdata/gravitylan and a restart help.
